html:
The Inca road system, called Qhapaq Ñan or "royal road" in Quechua, was a network of about 40,000 km of roads that held the Inca Empire together. Most of it was built or joined up between about 1438 and 1533.

Two main roads ran north to south, one along the coast and one, the most important, through the high Andes, with many branches between them. Builders paved the roads where needed, cut stairways into steep slopes, built retaining walls and drains, and hung rope bridges over gorges. Some routes reused older roads of the Wari and others.

The roads carried armies, officials, llama caravans and workers doing labour service, but no wheeled carts. Along them stood:

  • relay posts for the chasquis, runners who passed messages and quipu records from hand to hand, covering long distances in a few days;
  • tambos, way stations a day's walk apart, with food and lodging;
  • administrative centres with rows of storehouses (see Inca storehouses).

Use of the roads was controlled by the state; ordinary people needed permission to travel them. The network is often compared with the roads of the Roman Empire, built more than a thousand years earlier. After the Spanish conquest, the roads helped Pizarro reach Cusco, and parts fell into ruin as the colonial economy turned to mines like Potosí. Large sections survive, and in 2014 the network was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
sum: The Inca road system, called Qhapaq Ñan or "royal road" in Quechua, was a network of about 40,000 km of roads that held the Inca Empire together. Most of it was built or joined up between about 1438 and 1533.
